newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN chief, Ogata sound alarm bells on Central Africa.
newsitem.headline: UN chief, Ogata sound alarm bells on Central Africa.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Friday called for an emergency mission to go to Zaire followed by an international conference to prevent warfare spreading throughout central Africa.

But before a conference could be convened he said a "provisional solution" had to be found to end the fighting in eastern Zaire. He said he wanted to send a team with a new mediator. He has not yet chosen the mediator.
The Security Council, according to its current president, Gerardo Martinez Blanco of Honduras, called on all to stop fighting and start a political dialogue.

He said members supported the idea of a new mediator and "the possiblity of sending a high-level mission" to the region as well as beginning preparations for a conference if leaders in the area agreed.

Fighting is raging in eastern Zaire between ethnic Tutsis, who have lived in the country since the 18th century, and the Zairean army, which says Rwanda is helping the Tutsis. The United Nations fears the fighting could spread further with the help of Tutsi-dominated armies in Burundi and Rwanda.
The eastern Zaire region also is host to Hutus who fled Rwanda fearing revenge attacks after the 1994 massacre of up to a million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

"The war is not limited to Zaire and Rwanda," Boutros-Ghali said. "Refugees have left the camps and have spread through the region. Roads have been blocked and we are not able to offer assistance to the refugees."

The U.N. High Commission for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, who also briefed the council, said Tutsi forces were on the offensive and had virtually taken the city of Uvira. Some 220,000 refugees were on the move emptying 12 of her camps.
She said Hutu refugees might be safer going back to Rwanda, under UNHCR protection, but few trusted going home and were heading for mountains and banana plantations.
"I can do things to protect refugees, but I cannot stop the fighting and protect refugees in military conflicts," she said, adding: "Wish me good luck!"
Boutros-Ghali said he proposed an international conference as a medium-term solution and that Uganda and Rwanda, which originally had opposed such a meeting, had now agreed to one.

But he said the meeting needed preparation and should include "foreign actors who are playing a role in this tragedy in eastern Zaire." The large quantity of weapons in the region, he said, is "coming from outside," not from Africa.
U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright said the United States supported a mission to the area to ascertain the facts. She said she supported a conference only if it is well prepared.

British Ambassador Sir John Weston told reporters the situation increased the risk of a further disintegration of an important African nation, namely Zaire, and complicated the already volatile situation in Burundi.

"That's the analysis and I've heard nobody dispute that," he said, adding that nothing had been decided yet in the Security Council. But he said, "We are all clear that the nature of the fighting is accentuated by the fact there are too many arms washing around in the hands of the people who are going at each other."
Weston said several steps needed to be taken:
-- A humanitarian and political emergency plan, put together by Boutros-Ghali and his staff working closely with the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees.
-- A mission to the area, both to focus more sharply on the facts, and perhaps to play a political role.
-- Consideration of a regional conference.

He said the lead for the conference should come from regional leaders themselves "because we need to be clear on the objectives of any such conference and that it has the full support of the regional players before going beyond an early and preparatory stage."
